claim: Alzheimer disease (AD) is marked by structural and functional disruptions in the brain that can be observed through multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in preclinical and symptomatic stages of the disease.
source: Alzheimer disease (AD) is marked by structural and functional disruptions in the brain, some of which can be observed through multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in preclinical and symptomatic stages of the disease (Frisoni et al., 2010; Brier et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Frisoni et al., 2010; Brier et al., 2014a).

claim: Several studies have demonstrated that BAG is elevated in symptomatic AD.
source: Indeed, several studies have demonstrated that BAG is elevated (i.e. the brain 'appears older' than expected) in a host of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including symptomatic AD (Franke et al., 2010; Franke and Gaser, 2012; Gaser et al., 2013), as well as schizophrenia (e.g., Koutsouleris et al., 2014), HIV (e.g., Cole et al., 2017c), and type-2 diabetes (e.g., Franke et al., 2013), and moreover, predicts mortality (Cole et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies (Franke et al., 2010; Franke and Gaser, 2012; Gaser et al., 2013).

claim: BAG is elevated in schizophrenia.
source: Indeed, several studies have demonstrated that BAG is elevated (i.e. the brain 'appears older' than expected) in a host of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including symptomatic AD (Franke et al., 2010; Franke and Gaser, 2012; Gaser et al., 2013), as well as schizophrenia (e.g., Koutsouleris et al., 2014), HIV (e.g., Cole et al., 2017c), and type-2 diabetes (e.g., Franke et al., 2013), and moreover, predicts mortality (Cole et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Koutsouleris et al., 2014).

claim: Lower BAG is associated with lower risk of disease progression.
source: Conversely, lower BAG is associated with lower risk of disease progression (Gaser et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019; Bocancea et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Gaser et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019; Bocancea et al., 2021).

claim: BAG exceeds hippocampal volume and CSF biomarkers (pTau and Aβ42) in sensitivity to AD progression.
source: Critically, at least one comparison suggests that BAG exceeds other established MRI (hippocampal volume) and CSF (pTau and Aβ42) biomarkers in sensitivity to AD progression (Gaser et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Gaser et al., 2013).

claim: Symptomatic AD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) are associated with elevated BAG.
source: Several studies have established that symptomatic AD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) are associated with elevated BAG (Cole and Franke, 2017b; Franke and Gaser, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Cole and Franke, 2017b; Franke and Gaser, 2019).

claim: Greater BAG is associated with greater amyloid PET burden in a Down syndrome cohort.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that greater BAG is associated with greater amyloid PET burden in a Down syndrome cohort (Cole et al., 2017a) and with greater tau PET burden in sporadic MCI and symptomatic AD (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Cole et al., 2017a).

claim: Greater BAG is associated with greater tau PET burden in sporadic MCI and symptomatic AD.

claim: An amyloid-negative trained brain age model is more sensitive to progressive stages of AD than a typical amyloid-insensitive model.
source: Indeed, one recent study demonstrated that an amyloid-negative trained brain age model (Ly et al., 2020) is more sensitive to progressive stages of AD than a typical amyloid-insensitive model (Cole et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ly et al., 2020; Cole et al., 2015).

claim: Traditional and amyloid-negative trained brain age models were similarly related to molecular AD biomarkers.
source: Another recent comparison demonstrated that both traditional and amyloid-negative trained brain age models were similarly related to molecular AD biomarkers, but that further attempts to 'disentangle' AD from brain age by including more advanced AD continuum participants in the training sample significantly reduced relationships between brain age and AD markers (Hwang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Hwang et al., 2022).

claim: Including more advanced AD continuum participants in the training sample significantly reduced relationships between brain age and AD markers.

claim: The observed R2 of the multimodal model outperformed all R2 estimates from a bootstrapped distribution of models with randomly reshuffled FC features (p < 0.001).
source: The observed R2S+FC outperformed all R2 estimates from this bootstrapped distribution (p < 0.001; see Figure 1—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the modest increase in model performance observed in the stacked multimodal (S+FC) model over the unimodal structural model is due to meaningful age-related FC signal, rather than capitalizing on noise in a larger feature set.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Structural BAG was elevated by 5.10 years in CI participants compared to CN controls, which is comparable to previous structural age prediction models demonstrating elevations in AD and MCI samples between 5 and 10 years.

evidence: The claim is supported by data from the current study and citations to prior research (Cole and Franke, 2017b; Franke and Gaser, 2019).

evidence: The claim is supported by data from the current study and a citation to prior research (Millar et al., 2022).

claim: The combined reduction of FC-BAG in the presymptomatic stage and increase in the symptomatic stage suggest a biphasic functional response to AD progression.
source: The combined reduction of FC-BAG in the presymptomatic stage and increase in the symptomatic stage suggest a biphasic functional response to AD progression, which is partially consistent with some prior suggestions (Jagust and Mormino, 2011; Jones et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2017; Schultz et al., 2017; Wales and Leung, 2021; see Millar et al., 2022 for a more detailed discussion).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior research (Jagust and Mormino, 2011; Jones et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2017; Schultz et al., 2017; Wales and Leung, 2021; Millar et al., 2022).

evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by a citation to prior research (Cabeza et al., 2018).

claim: Greater structural and multimodal BAG estimates were associated with lower cognitive performance within the CI participants, consistent with previous reports.
source: Although FC-BAG was not associated with individual differences in a global cognitive composite within any of our analysis samples, greater structural and multimodal BAG estimates were associated with lower cognitive performance within the CI participants. Hence, these estimates may be sensitive markers of cognitive decline in the symptomatic stage. This finding is consistent with previous reports that other structural brain age estimates are associated with cognitive performance in AD (Eavani et al., 2018), Down syndrome (Cole et al., 2017a), HIV (Petersen et al., 2021; Petersen et al., 2022), as well as cognitively normal controls (Richard et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the current study and citations to prior research (Eavani et al., 2018; Cole et al., 2017a; Petersen et al., 2021; Petersen et al., 2022; Richard et al., 2018).
